Visiting Mihintale was an unforgettable experience! The moment you arrive, you’re greeted by serene surroundings and a sense of history that feels almost tangible. Climbing the steps to the summit was a little challenging, but every step was worth it for the breathtaking views of the surrounding Anuradhapura plains. The ancient Buddhist ruins, including the monasteries, stupas, and the sacred Bodhi tree, reflect the deep spiritual significance of this place. The Mihintale rock carvings and the bell tower are particularly impressive, offering a glimpse into the craftsmanship of ancient Sri Lanka. What I loved most was the peaceful ambiance; it’s easy to feel a sense of calm and reflection here. Make sure to bring water, wear comfortable shoes, and allocate a few hours to fully explore the site. The sunrise from the top is absolutely magical and worth waking up early for! Highly recommend this spot for history enthusiasts, pilgrims, or anyone looking to experience Sri Lanka’s cultural heritage. Mihintale is a true gem that combines spirituality, history, and natural beauty.

Lovely place to visit. Try to get there early before the tout groups arrive and the rocks get too hot. You need to take your shoes off before you get to the terrace and the steps are not very smooth. Once on the terrace you can climb a fairly steep rock to a peak with excellent views. The climb is not too strenuous but does require cooperation between ascenders and descenders. It is quite slippery coming down, There is a higher terrace with a couple of huge stupas and also a third climb to the large Buddha statue. Lots of interesting things in addition to these. Be wary of getting food out of your bag - the monkeys will be on you immediately. All in all, well worth a visit.

We arranged a tour to visit the religious sites in and around Anuradhapura. "Mihintale" is one of the sites we visited. Mihinthale is a mountain in Sri Lanka near Anuradhapura. Its a pilgrimage site for the Buddhists in Sri Lanka, and worshippers around the world. Let me give a brief description of "Mihintale". It has some some religious monuments, and some ruins. Buddhists visit "Mihintale" during the weekends, during special hoildays, or on full moon poya days. This place is always with visitors, local and foreign. Specially in June, on the full moon poya day we could see many pilgrims visit "Mihintale" to make their pilgrimage, and then proceed towards Anuradhapura. It has a story of Thera Mahinda who came to Sri Lanka and met King Devanampiyatissa, and preached the Buddhist doctrine, as per books written by authors. There are many books written by authors about the historical places in Sri Lanka, including Mihintale, Anuradhapura, Polonnaruwa, and other places etc. In Mihintale we could see a small Dagaba, with some stone pillars, a large Stupa known as the "Maha Seya" and a Buddha Statue on the summit of the Mihintale hill. It takes about 15 to 20 minutes to climb the mountain peak. The best time to climb is early morning, so that you could see the sunrise. or in the late afternoon when the sun is not that hot, and see the sunset. These are the best times to climb, as you may get dehydrated. You are advised to take a bottle of water to refresh yourself. Wear proper clothing, as no body parts be exposed. Photography is allowed, but if you are to photographing for a reason, you will need to take permission from the authorities at the site office.  You are not allowed to take photographs with your back shown to the Statue, Dagaba, or the Stupa. I recommend anyone, local or foreign tourists to visit Mihintale, and experience the climb, view of the landscapes, and the sunrise or the sunset from the peak of Mihintale. Anyone would love and enjoy the fleet of steps that makes you climb to the peak. All are welcome to be at Mihintale and enjoy the experience. Will be back with another historic site sooooon. "Flavorful Destinations" By:- M N Nizam

East of Anuradhapura, this fabled site was where Mahinda, a relative of Ashoka, the Buddhist ruler of India, met the local king Devanampiya Tissa in 247 BC. After the latter successfully answered the riddle of the mangoes, Mahinda provided teachings of the Buddha. The setting is rugged, quite apart from the 1,850 possible steps to be climbed to see everything. The upper terrace has the most important areas associated with the site, a small dagoba or stupa marking the spot of the meeting. The higher up Mahaseya Dagoba reputedly holds a single hair of the Buddha. There are great views from this level and also the Aradhana Gala, a rock face with iron railings, the location of Mahinda’s first sermon. The upper terrace needs to be done barefoot and without a hat. It will be worth your while.

According to legend, it was at Mihintale – literally “Mahinda’s Hill” – that the Indian missionary Mahinda, met and converted King Devanampiyatissa in 247 BC, establishing Buddhism as the island’s state religion. Mahinda was the son of the great Mauryan emperor Asoka, sent by his father to bring word of the Buddha’s teachings to Sri Lanka. Buddhism was immediately embraced with fervour by the Sinhalese people and soon became firmly established in the island – unlike in India, its birthplace, where it would subsequently fall into terminal decline. Mihintale, on a higher plane All over the world, high places are given religious significance, with the result that devotees are always climbing steps. Sometimes on their knees. Mihintale is one such place, its various shrines connected by a total of some 1,840 steps that ultimately lead to the summit – steep enough to require deep breaths and a meditative pace. They were built in the reign of Bhathika Abhaya (22 BC–AD 7), although a later paved road provides a short cut up to the first level.there have so many histrionically place in here

We visited Mihintale for a couple of hours while travelling between Anuradhapura and Sigiriya and it was well worth the stop. There are four main components to the complex at Mihintale and three require climbing up steps/rocks so it's not a good option for anyone with impaired mobility.  The centrepiece in Mihintale is the Ambasthale Dagoba which is where a former King is said to have converted to buddhism. Up some steps to  one side of the main Dagoba is a relatively new white statue of buddha which looks great against the blue sky. On another side is the large Mahaseya Dagoba which offers good views across the area. We visited when it was offering time so were treated to a bit of ceremony. Then there is a tricky rock to climb (especially if you are wearing socks as it can be a bit slippy so think about taking them off briefly) which gives wonderful 360 views of the site and surrounding area, all the way back to Anuradhapura, where you can see varous dagobas in the skyline. On the way back down we stopped at Sinha Pokuna to see the lion carving. Its a wonderful and fascinating site and would be a great place to be for sunrise or sunset

Unless you want to prove something to yourself, there is no need to climb all 1800+ steps. Ask your driver to take you up Old Road, which gets you almost halfway up. That leaves only a few hundred steps to climb. Bring water. The ruins at the level of the ticket booth (at the end of Old Road, halfway up the hill) are good for a 15-minute walk-around. The stone canoe at the “alms house” is quite impressive. Apparently, lay people would fill this with rice as donation to the monks who lived here. Don’t miss the lion carved into the side of Lion Rock. Up the hill, there are three peaks forming a triangle around a basin. The basin is not large -- little bigger than a football field. The lowest peak has an imposing modern statue of the Buddha – very easy climb, but not much by way of views from there. The second peak has a huge white stupa; good views from there, especially of the other peaks. The tallest is a steep climb up bare rock (steps cut into the rock with handrails). Great views, but dangerously slippery if wet. Because it’s a sacred place, you have to take off your shoes as you approach the three peaks and basin. Wear old socks if you’re not accustomed to walking on paving stones or sand that is frying-pan hot from the tropical sun. Even if not hot, the sharp grit underfoot makes it painful. Th historical significance of this place has to do with being where a king first accepted Buddhism. Entry was 500 rupees. The site does not seem to have any cafe, toilet or shop selling water -- but then again, I didn't look that carefully. Covering the upper steps and peaks leisurely takes only about 90 minutes. To escape the worst of midday sun, you can start the climb at 4pm and still have plenty of light when you reach the top. But there are plenty of shrine-caves and ruins in the area. If you are intent on visiting them, I think you will need an hour or two more, which means starting much earlier than 4pm. I didn’t bother, as by this point in my visit to the country, I’ve had my fill of Buddhist places. My hotel arranged a tuktuk from Anuradhapura for 4 hours at a cost of 2,000 rupees (leaving little time for shrine-caves). It’s only 13km or 30 minutes journey time. The driver took me to a few other places before reaching the Mihintale peaks. One was a “big tree” monastery (nothing much to see except a big tree and a human skeleton); another was the site of a “hospital” dated to about 800 CE (OK for a 10-minute walk-around); and the third was “Black Water Pool” (more ruins, so-so views). If your hotel does not offer such a service, it’s still very easy to hire a tutktuk from anywhere in Anuradhapura for 3 to 4 hours for a similar price.

As it is of religious significance, shoulders and legs should be covered and no hats.  My tip would be, if in doubt carry a wrap/sarong/shawl. You have to visit and make it to the top of the rock . Just be aware of the monkeys which can be a bit aggressive if you get too close to them. I recommend to you to visit Minintale.

Every year in month of Poson (June) Buddhists visit this area. King constructed many Viharas & caves for monks. Car parking is at lower level but bigger buses go to next level where ticket window is located. There are 1840 granite steps to view it completely. At lower level you find a place called Refractory probably a place to store cooked food, two stone troughs ,large one for rice & smaller for curry. There are many spots for grinding spices. Above it a place having two granite inscriptions telling us records of payments to service staff. After further climbing you come to a plain platform area where you have to remove your shoes for further visit. There is a temple in center of this area. Now 3 peaks to climb One is having a Maha Stupa, no clear steps,climb with help of railing, 7-19 AD Another peak called Aradhana Gala) where Mahinda landed. Difficult for senior citizens to climb. Now it became famous important Buddhist pilgrimage site in Sri Lanka, which consists of several religious monuments. The first meeting of introducing Buddhism to  King Devanampiyatissa the by a Buddhist monk Mahinda, migrated from India,  who was the son of Emperor Asoka(268 –  232 BC), an Indian emperor of the Maurya Dynasty,  subsequently,  inaugurated the presence of Buddhism in Sri Lanka. Buddhist devotees strongly believe that the  team of Buddhist missioners, who considerd as  envoys of the king, had flown  to Mihintale rock from India by their spiritual power.   Legends state Emperor Asoka converted to Buddhism, after witnessing the mass deaths of the Kalinga War of India. These  are certain historical information connected with Mihintale. As the legend, In Sinhala (Sri Lanka main language ) “Mihin-Thalé” literally means the “plateau of Mihindu”. This is a flat terrain on top of a Mihintale rock, from where the  was supposed to have called King Devanampiyatissa, by the King’s first name to stop him shooting a deer in jungle.

Once you have responded to conversation they have become your unwanted helpers at an undisclosed fee. As stated earlier, the climb to the pinnacle is quite arduous as one has to climb using small steps carved into the rock (there is a handrail to the top). A beautiful and serene place where Mahinda, son of the Indian King Asoka, converted King Devanampiya Tissa to Buddhism in 3rd century BC. This "sacred Hill of Mihintale" is less visited than the sites of Polonnaruwa and Anuradhapura, but should be a must see because of its history, scenery and serenity. Visit in the morning preferably as it gets very hot. No shoes allowed. The visit should take a couple of hours with a good guide. For the more daring, a climb to Aradhana Gala (Meditation Rock) is worth the effort (it is very steep on narrow steps - remove your socks if you kept them as the steps carved out of the rock can be slippery). From the top, the view over the plain, the Dagoba and the Buddha statue is breathtaking.

my driver recommended me to visit it at this time of the afternoon to avoid the midday heat. The Stairway is a series of flights, 1843 ancient granite slab steps lead majestically up the hillside. On the second landing I took on the services of a guide (Rs 1000), it is also where the monks’ refectory is located with huge stone troughs that the lay followers kept filled with rice for the monks. Nearby, at a place identified as the mon¬astery’s relic house, are two inscribed stone slabs erected during the reign of King Ma¬hinda IV. The final steep stairway, lined with frangipani trees, leads to the place where Mahinda and the king met. The Am¬basthale Dagoba is built over the spot where Mahinda stood. The bodhi tree to the left of the base of the steps is said to be one of the oldest surviving ones. From here there is a fantastic view over the lakes and trees to Anuradhapu¬ra, a horizon studded with the domes and spikes of all the massive dagobas. The guide did prove valuable as he had to race back up the steps to retrieve my camera that I had left on a bench whilst putting my sandals back on. There were also plenty of resident Macquae Monkeys, Langur Monkeys and a lone giant squirrel.

For 500 LKR you can wander around on 582 acres. There is several beautiful places - several with a spectacular view of the surroundings. At this location, an old mango Forrest, King Devenampiyathissa met Arahath Mahinda Thero, a Buddhist enlightened monk from India. The monk introduced buddhism to the king and told him to stop hunting the animals that roam the forrest. The king was only there to administrate the earth. Being a few km outside of Anuradhapura a lot of tourists miss this site. If at all possible, do not make the same mistake. It is quite simply the most breathtaking historic religious site we visited in our two week stay in Sri Lanka. There is a board at the bottom of the hill very helpfully stating there are 1800 steps. This may be true in a manner of speaking, but please do not be put off - it is not necessary to do anywhere near that many. From the car park there is a short sloping road up to the ticket office level, and then there are about 200 steps (mostly shaded) to the 'Take your shoes off' cabin (as with every temple in SL take thick socks to avoid burnt feet and constantly dodging sharp stones). From there it's only about 30 more to the central stupa area. This area is shady and relaxing. From this level you can climb to a stunning white buddha (probably only about 50 steps but as they are carved into the rock some are a bit awkward so take care - there is a handrail however). You could also climb from the central area up to the big stupa, that's about another 200 steps (shaded) but definitely worth it for the stunning views and the cool breeze! There are also options from the central area to climb up to sunset rock (we didn't bother, it looked crowded and was nowhere near sunset - the views can't be all that different from the big stupa) and down to some kind of cave art - we got halfway down and gave up as we couldn't face climbing all the way back up afterwards! Please note if you are THAT kind of tourist, there are no sweetie shops, hot dog stands or kiddies playparks here. It is a historical religious site. If you want those things, stay at home. Otherwise, if you can handle the steps (which as stated above are not as numerous as claimed) this place is magical and worth a few hours of anyone's time. Do take your socks and some water though.

If you're not afraid of climbing a few steps, then you'll be rewarded not only with a wonderful view, but also a temple that is worth visiting. Tourist pay 500 LKR that is worth it. Also visit nearby black pond and monk meditation quarters under rocks in a lush forest!

This climb starts off as fairly easy until you reach the first plateau.  You then have three choices for further climbs. On the advice of our guide, I chose the difficult rock climb first. To get up to the rock you need to navigate up a staircase built into the stone, with a handrail available in the difficult spots. It's quite steep and some of the carved steps are only an inch or two deep, so you need to take it slowly and surely.  Once you reach the top and make it to the narrow platform area the views are spectacular. Going down can be a bit problematic if you are competing for space for those ascending.  It's advisable to hold the handrail at all times but sometimes this isn't possible.  Even if you are wearing walking shoes it can be a bit slippy.  Our guide said barefoot was best but then the rock can get very hot in the sun.  It's one of those descents where you are glad to reach the bottom. After that it's easy to ascend to the temple area using conventional steps. Here the views are almost as good and there is no difficulty to overcome. All in all this is a good complex with spectacular views from the highest spots.

This ancient site, the cradle of Sri Lankan Buddhism, is a lovely place to visit.  It isn't far from the better known site of Anuradhapura, and is well worth visiting as well.  It may not be World Heritage listed, but it is nice and nicer than many places that are. There are a lot of steps leading up to the site - almost 2000 in all.  However if you have transport, you can be driven up to quite near the top and only climb a few of them.  I am unfit and found it perfectly fine climbing from there, I suspect the full climb would be all right too if you started early and took it at a gentle pace. The site consists of several interesting buildings; the ruins of a monastery, two pagodas, a small museum, and a giant sitting Buddha.  There is also a steep rocky viewpoint which can be climbed if you don't mind a bit of a scramble.  The views are wonderful, looking out over the countryside. The area has great religious significance for Buddhists as it is believed to be the site where the first Buddhist king of Sri Lanka was converted to the religion by a group of monks.  The spot where he met the monks is marked by a tree and a nearby very small museum. As it is a religious site, you need to remove your shoes before the final set of steps and leave them with the shoe attendants.  You may keep your socks on, which is a good idea as the ground gets hot here in the open sun.  You should also ensure your shoulders and legs to below the knee are covered.  Hats also need to be removed.  There is limited shade at the top so be sure to where plenty of suncream or take a scarf (which is permitted). I'd highly recommend this site for a visit as it is beautiful and interesting.  It would not be a good place to visit in the rain though as the climb to the top of the viewpoint would be dangerous in wet conditions I think, and the views may not be so good.  It's also quite exposed.  I think children would like it, as there's lots to see.  It's also less crowded than many of the sites I visited in the region and has a peaceful feeling even when there are plenty of people around.

I with a group of 22 friends from Thailand, including 3 Buddhist Monks, visited Mihinthale on January 13th, 2015 morning. Mihinthale means plateau of Mahinda or Mihindu This place considered by Sri Lankan Buddhists as one of the most sacred place as the Arhath Mahinda Thero, a son of the emperor Ashoka, India,  a Buddhist Monk, came to establish Buddhism here in Sri Lanka. This is very calm and quite forestry rock mountain area about 300 meters above sea level and spread  over more than 800 acres. Lots of caves and ruins of old constructions can see here and there. Most are built with huge granite pillars and slabs joining very neatly. You have to climb about 1000 granite steps not very steep built around 340BC.  Main places you can see are the Alms Hall, Hospital, 3 stupas, Aradhana Gala(Rock), Mihindu Guhawa(cave), Refectory and the Kalu Diya Pokuna(pond). It is really worth to visit but keep in mind go during morning or evening to enjoy the comfort of environment and skip the month of June as huge number of local pilgrimages crowded here.

The intimate temple at the foot of the Mahaseya Dagoba is popular with local pilgrims and a welcome, serene spot to catch your breath and ponder the importance of this anciant site. Not to be missed.

Well worth a visit and a short distance from Anuradhapura, a climb up steps is required at this excellent site.  Your choice of several hundred from the very bottom, or drive up to a carpark and climb up a beautiful and comfortable gradient of a couple of hundred steps flanked by asala trees.  The site is covered by the ruins of a huge vihara, ancient hospital and ponds and the mountaintop surmounted by stupas and rupas reached by further steps cut into rock.  The views from the top are tremendous and worth the trek alone.

This place was by far my fav ruin in sri lanka and the pool of the dark water I believe it is called is absolutely breathtaking. It's unbelievable. If u have to choose amongst the ruins (Andrahapura or pollunawara) choose here. It's serenly beautiful. The other ruins in minthale are wonderful too but this place blew me away

We visited Mihintale in a "backpacker experience", and really enjoyed it. Several from the team preferred it than Anuradhapura; I think both are worth visiting, with the advantage that Mihintale is much cheaper! Some recommendations: it can be visited from Anura by bike, although we didn't do this. We did however go by bus, taking it from Anura in direction of Trincomalee (there aren't many, for some strange reason). I believe the first one was around 08.00 but check with your GH. Once there, you can either walk or take a bus/tuk tuk to avoid the first stairs, and just beside the place where you buy the tickets you can ask to leave your bags in a hut with a policeman! Nothing was asked for but this can probably change -and just for security sake don't leave any valuables just in case. With 2 or 3 hours you have plenty of time to climb, visit the dagobas, enjoy the amazing view and go back down. And at 12.30 more or less, there is another bus to Trincomalee - so it's a smart way to combine both things!

breathtaking views and fascinating temples some practical advice: I have been there on a hot day in August, and muggy, absolutely recommended hat and sun cream for sensitive skin, maybe even an umbrella. Buddhist temples you enter without shoes and with your knees and shoulders covered, I recommend dressing in keeping this site because in the cover up with a sarong would be inconvenient, you will probably climb a hill and there are several steps to deal with bare feet, the stones, however, are hot so I suggest a pair of socks in the most do not have to reuse later (there is also sand over the stones and leaves)

I went up at sunset which was beautiful to appreciate the colors of the sunset reflecting off the Buddha and stupa, which is also lit up. The highlight was walking to a lookout point above the stupa, appreciating the surrounding countryside and summer breeze.

To reach the summit you need to climb around 1800 stairs, some of them do not offer the best grip. Do not miss the ticket counter at the base of the first section of steps! It is to the right and easily missed as there is no signage. Having said all this, the place is extremely peaceful. It offers magnificent views.

Buddhism was apparently introduced to Sri Lanka at the spot of the small "mango" Dagoda, also the second oldest one in Sri Lanka. I would recommend getting an official guide, only five of them around this site. Guides will give a good introduction to the site, pointing out certain interesting spots. Even without them, take a look around the old site of the monastery which was destroyed by the Indian Chola Dynasty. Go up to the big pagoda, the view is awesome, miles and miles of flat land all around! It's no wonder why the ancients wanted to move to a more defensible place!

Greatly designed area which has been built more than two millenia ago. Modern day excavations still ongoing. More descriptive information would have been more welcome to the uninitiated visitor. An interesting climb, a venerated place of worship for Buddhists.

AMAZING! Great value (especially compared to the expensive Anuradhapura ruins). Not a lot of tourists - was mostly pilgrims, which was a lovely thing to witness! It's a beautiful climb up the mountain side and the sites at the top are breathtaking. Lots of monkeys - Every monkey has a different haircut.

If you travel to Anuradhapura, you just have to go to Mihintale. This is a bit far away from Anuradhapura city, and this place alone is better than any other sites in the Central Anuradhapura Archaeological site. We went there by bus early in the morning from Anuradhapura city. The bus number was 835. It took us less than an hour, and cost 30 LKR for each person. The entry fee of this place was 500 LKR per person. You need to buy the ticket before starting the climb to the Great stairways. But before that, dont forget to miss out the other places, including 68 caves, lion pond, etc... 68 caves is an amazing place. Its an amazing adventure when you just keep going further and further, and caves after caves, they just dont seem to end. When you reach the mountain top, leave your shoes at the shoe rack, or inside your bag. Then you 4 places to visit. A doguba at the center, buddha statue on the left, mihintale rock straight ahear, and another large doguba on right. Climbing to the top of Mihintale rock is a superb adventure, and view from there is simply amazing. When you are climbing down from mountain top, just after the great stairways, turn left, and you will find a secret path to "Eth Vehara". Eth Vehara is the hightest point in Mihintale mountain. There is a small doguba on top. And the stairways are ancient, decayed, and risky. Its not very safe. But you should try out if you are interested. On you way down from Eth Vehara, when you reach the junction where there is a sign board describing "Eth vehara", find a secret stairways going up towards the opposite direction of Eth vehara. Follow this path, and you will reach "Naga pokuna". This is a very beautiful lake on the edge of a big piece of rock. Really a beautiful place to travel. Overall, we really really liked Mihintale, and u must say, dont leave Anuradhapura before visiting Mihintale.

Situated 30 mins (by bus) off from the Anuradhapura town.. this is by far the best of places.. not just in Anuradhapura or Sri Lanka.. but maybe in the world. More than what is AT the the TOP, what is on WAY to the TOP is most fascinating. I hired a guide who was well informed to show me the "60/64 (?) Caves of Mihintale" on the way to the top.. a series of natural caves on drop down slopes.. where monks used to meditate. A stone inscription can also be found here.. considered on of the first written texts of the island (disputed). The caves are on 3 staggered levels.. and this is better than the stupas (locally known as "dagoba") on the top. I climbed on the hanging ledges.. and both the view and the thrill of the caves is out of this world. But beware of monkeys (the reddish-white faced ones) as they move in packs and tend to attach bagpacks for food.. I was almost attacked. =/ Also en route to the top is the ancient monastery with interesting ancient halls and structures...  And on the top is a stunning white stupa.. the climb is easy and pleasant.. for those with soft feet.. socks are advisable.. carry plenty of water as it can get quite hot.. A guide is advisable because everything way more interesting with the history explained a bit.. My guide Amara was very friendly, helpful and honest.. with a very good command over English (also knows German and French)  charged me very reasonably.. owns a tuk tuk and has very good knowledge on the history and knows of several places that are superb yet not mentioned in most travel sites / books (Amara : + 94 0712571472)..without him I would not find the "hidden things" that I understood would be missed out easily..

Interesting information, plus great photos of the before / after restoration works.

We recently visitrd Anuradhapura as part of an arcgaeological tour and Harvard about this site which had been deleted from our itinerary presumably because of the stairs (1890).  Yet given its significance to the history of the island and our lack of issue with the stairs at Sigiriya and the high ratings at Trip Advisor, we gave it a try. First off it was a short twenty minute drive from Anuradhapura and the parking lot is at a level which eliminates 800 steps.  For those steps that remain, my wife referred to them as a "ramp with steps" --in other words, they are easy. If there were no remains at the site, the view of Anuradhapura in the distance with its tanks and stupas would be worth it.  Our highlights included a stupa at a lower level with well preserved frontispieces that gave us a better idea as to how it's larger cousins at Anuradhapura appeared.  The remains of the monastery with the stone hewn rice and curry troughs and the hospital with the sarcophagus-like bath for Ayurdavedic treatments were fascinating.  The true highlight was the Kaludiya Pokuna, the "Dark Water Pond" which is an outlier quite close to the main site.  Remains of a monastic cave with window carvings evocative of Angkor and a large man made pool that reflects the dark stone walls of the surrounding cliffs and the remains of a pavilion jutting into the water made my wife ask me to leave her there to be picked up prior to returning to Canada. In all, this site was a wonderful way to spend two to three hours.  We were even invited to tour a living monastery next to the site.  There are knowledgeable guides on site.

We really enjoyed our time here and it was made all the more special by the fantastic guide who approached us as we arrived, to offer his services. I'm sure he was working with our tuk tuk driver but it didn't matter as his knowledge and information was so good. I would definitely recommend keeping your socks on as the ground is baking hot. You can buy water at the top of the stair climb to the dagoba as well as ice creams and cool drinks. We had been to the sights at Anuradhupura but actually enjoyed Mihinitale more for its variety and compactness. The frangipanis were beautiful and we also saw birds and other wild life along the way. Pretty views across the forests. Just remember that you'll be taking off your shoes and hats a few times so wear something easy and have socks in your bag.

If you had an extra 2 hours and wanted to take your chances the last climb is for you. Around to the rear left of the Buddha at the top is a little climb with spectacular views.  The area around the enormous stupa also offers wonderful views.As much of this area is sacred, it is a no shoes zone.  Socks are tolerated for we westerners with soft feet.

We hired a tuk tuk to take us out to Mihintale and back from Anuradhapura - it takes only 3 so hours to climb and explore the many various and interesting places within the sacred site. We were met by a guide and, after a bit of convincing from him, we decided to hire him (850 SRP for three or so hours). I am so thankful we hired a guide - our experience of this place would've been so different without him; we learned so much during his exhaustive tour of various areas, and his knowledge was extensive. Mihintale is internationally recognized as one of Sri Lanka's most sacred sites, and we went here particularly to spend time in meditation.  Buddhism was introduced here by the Arahat Mahinda around 3000 BCE. I and my daughter went early in the morning, and were pleased that unlike the other sites we visited, there were no touts or vendors crowding the entrance.  Later we learned that the current chief monk Ven. Dhammarathana Thero was making efforts to preserve the sanctity of the place. The beautiful views from the lookout resonated with peace and tranquility, as did the areas around the caves where the Arahats in the past meditated.  We saw a variety of birds, several monkeys and some squirrels.  There were no mosquitoes at all.  The place was quite clean. It was a joy to meditate here  and enjoy the powerful, sacred energy of the place. Crystal enthusiasts like us would also be delighted to see the very large scepter-shaped quartz terminator that used to be on top of the dagoba.  This was hit by lightning in April 2010, and is now in Mihintale's relic room. Mihintale has the unique distinction of being the only religious site in the world with 2 dagobas, the Ambasthale dagoba which was built on the site where Mahinda met the king, and the other on the mountain behind it. Mihintale is about 30 minutes away from Anuradhapura, and is about a 5 minute tuktuk ride away from the town center.  Definitely worth a visit.

We arrived in time to visit the ruins and get to the top for sunset which was a good move as it wasn't too hot and the dagoba oozed atmosphere. We hired a guide at the bottom which made the visit more interesting.  He was knowledgable and fairly entertaining  The site has an interesting history and the views from the top are wonderful.  The walk up is quite steep but manageable and definitely worth the effort.  The number of steps can be reduced by getting a lift up the road. This was the highlight of our trip to Anurandhapura. We got a three wheeler from Anuradhapura which was a fun if slow way to get there.

Situated 12 kilometers east of the ruins of the great city of Anuradhapura, the sacred mountain of Mihintale is considered the location where Buddhism was first introduced to the island of Sri Lanka. According to historical sources, in the middle of the third century BC the great Indian Emperor Ashoka had sent his son Mahinda to Sri Lanka to spread the teachings of the Buddha. Mahinda and his group of Buddhist monks were camped upon the sides of Mt Mihintale when King Devanampiya Tissa of Anuradhapura encountered them during a royal hunting expedition. Mahinda spoke to the king of Buddhism. The date of this meeting between King Devanampiya Tissa and the Buddhist monk is believed to have been on the full moon of June in the year 247 BC. Soon thereafter the king (and 40,000 inhabitants of Anuradhapura) converted to Buddhism. An alternate story of the arrival of Buddhism in Sri Lanka tells that the Buddha himself journeyed to the island, on the back of the great winged demigod Garuda, but there is no historical evidence that the Buddha himself ever visited the island. Today the peak of Mihintale, approached by a grand stairway of 1840 granite steps, has many temples, lodgings for monks and several splendid statues of the Buddha. Each June on the full moon there is a pilgrimage commemorating the date when Mahinda first preached the Buddhist doctrine in Sri Lanka and many thousands of pilgrims flock from all over Sri Lanka to meditate on the holy peak.
